statement: Code that runs is not the same as a correct analysis, so researchers must check every step an AI agent takes.
Data leakage can make a machine-learning model look much better than it really is, so AI-built models should always be tested on truly unseen data.
AI analysis tools that produce readable, rerunnable code are more trustworthy than tools that just hand you an answer.
When AI tests many analysis options, researchers should report all of them, not just the ones that worked.
How well an LLM helps with statistics depends a lot on the model and the prompt, so one good result should not be assumed to hold for other tools.
AI will make p-hacking much worse, because trying thousands of analyses now takes almost no effort.
Used openly, AI can make science more robust by mapping every reasonable analysis instead of just the one a researcher picks.
Any result where AI helped choose the model should be labeled exploratory, never confirmatory.
An AI system that rates depression about as accurately as a human evaluator is ready to support real clinical decisions.
Students should learn to run analyses by hand before they are allowed to use AI data science agents.
